events.label: Holmes speaks about the strangeness of life

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: life is infinitely stranger than anything which the mind of man could invent; the things which are really mere commonplaces of existence would be unconceived; if we could fly out of the window and look down, it would make all fiction stale and unprofitable.

events.label: Watson replies that he is not convinced

communicates.speaker: doctor_watson
communicates.content: I am not convinced of it.

events.label: Holmes comments on police reports and realism

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The cases in the papers are bald and vulgar; police reports are realism pushed to its extreme limits; a realistic effect requires selection and discretion; the commonplace is unnatural.

events.label: Watson smiles and shakes his head
Watson agrees that Holmes's view is understandable

communicates.speaker: doctor_watson
communicates.content: I can quite understand your thinking so.

events.label: Watson describes Holmes's role and presents the newspaper

communicates.speaker: doctor_watson
communicates.content: Your position is that of unofficial adviser and helper to everybody who is absolutely puzzled throughout three continents; let us put it to a practical test; here is the first heading: 'A husband's cruelty to his wife.'

events.label: Watson predicts the newspaper case is familiar

communicates.speaker: doctor_watson
communicates.content: The account is perfectly familiar; there is the other woman, the drink, the push, the blow, the bruise, and the sympathetic sister or landlady; the crudest of writers could invent nothing more crude.

events.label: Holmes identifies the Dundas separation case and corrects Watson

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: This is the Dundas separation case; I was engaged in clearing up some small points in connection with it; the husband was a teetotaler, there was no other woman, and he had drifted into the habit of taking out his false teeth and hurling them at his wife; take a pinch of snuff and acknowledge that I have scored over you in your example.

events.label: Holmes holds out his snuffbox
Holmes explains the snuffbox souvenir

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I had not seen you for some weeks; the snuffbox is a little souvenir from the King of Bohemia in return for my assistance in the case of the Irene Adler papers.

events.label: Watson asks about the ring

communicates.speaker: doctor_watson
communicates.content: And the ring?

events.label: Holmes explains the ring's origin

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It was from the reigning family of Holland, though the matter in which I served them was of such delicacy that I cannot confide it even to you.

events.label: Watson asks whether Holmes has any case on hand

communicates.speaker: doctor_watson
communicates.content: Have you any on hand just now?

events.label: Sherlock Holmes stands at the window and looks down into the London street
A large woman crosses the road and rings the bell at the window
Sherlock Holmes comments on the woman's symptoms and infers a love matter

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I have seen those symptoms before. Oscillation upon the pavement always means an affaire de coeur. She would like advice, but is not sure that the matter is not too delicate for communication. When a woman has been seriously wronged by a man she no longer oscillates, and the usual symptom is a broken bell wire. Here we may take it that there is a love matter, but that the maiden is not so much angry as perplexed, or grieved. But here she comes in person to resolve our doubts.

events.label: Miss Mary Sutherland is announced and enters the room
Sherlock Holmes welcomes Miss Mary Sutherland, closes the door, bows her into an armchair, and looks her over
Sherlock Holmes asks whether typewriting is trying with short sight

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Do you not find that with your short sight it is a little trying to do so much typewriting?

events.label: Miss Mary Sutherland answers that she can type without looking at the letters

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: I did at first, but now I know where the letters are without looking.

events.label: Miss Mary Sutherland reacts with fear and astonishment
Miss Mary Sutherland says that Holmes has heard about her

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: You've heard about me, Mr. Holmes, else how could you know all that?

events.label: Sherlock Holmes says it is his business to know things and asks why she came to consult him

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Never mind. It is my business to know things. Perhaps I have trained myself to see what others overlook. If not, why should you come to consult me?

events.label: Miss Mary Sutherland says she came from Mrs. Etherege and asks Holmes to find Mr. Hosmer Angel

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: I came to you, sir, because I heard of you from Mrs. Etherege, whose husband you found so easy when the police and everyone had given him up for dead. Oh, Mr. Holmes, I wish you would do as much for me. I'm not rich, but still I have a hundred a year in my own right, besides the little that I make by the machine, and I would give it all to know what has become of Mr. Hosmer Angel.

events.label: Sherlock Holmes asks why Miss Mary Sutherland came in such a hurry

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Why did you come away to consult me in such a hurry?

events.label: Mary Sutherland explains why she came to Holmes

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: Yes, I did bang out of the house, for it made me angry to see the easy way in which Mr. Windibank—that is, my father—took it all. He would not go to the police, and he would not go to you, and so at last, as he would do nothing and kept on saying that there was no harm done, it made me mad, and I just on with my things and came right away to you.

events.label: Holmes asks whether Windibank is Mary Sutherland's father

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Your father, your stepfather, surely, since the name is different.

events.label: Mary Sutherland confirms that Windibank is her stepfather

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: Yes, my stepfather. I call him father, though it sounds funny, too, for he is only five years and two months older than myself.

events.label: Holmes asks whether Mary Sutherland's mother is alive

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: And your mother is alive?

events.label: Mary Sutherland says that her mother is alive and well

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: Oh, yes, mother is alive and well.

events.label: Mary Sutherland describes her father's death and the business's sale

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: I wasn’t best pleased when she married again so soon after father’s death, and a man who was nearly fifteen years younger than herself. Father was a plumber in the Tottenham Court Road, and he left a tidy business behind him, which mother carried on with Mr. Hardy, the foreman; but when Mr. Windibank came he made her sell the business, for he was very superior, being a traveller in wines. They got £4700 for the goodwill and interest, which wasn’t near as much as father could have got if he had been alive.

events.label: Holmes asks about Mary Sutherland's income

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Your own little income, does it come out of the business?

events.label: Mary Sutherland explains that her income came from her uncle Ned

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: Oh, no, sir. It is quite separate and was left me by my uncle Ned in Auckland. It is in New Zealand stock, paying 4 1/2 per cent. Two thousand five hundred pounds was the amount, but I can only touch the interest.

events.label: Holmes comments on Mary Sutherland's finances

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You interest me extremely. And since you draw so large a sum as a hundred a year, with what you earn into the bargain, you no doubt travel a little and indulge yourself in every way. I believe that a single lady can get on very nicely upon an income of about £60.

events.label: Mary Sutherland explains that Windibank draws her interest and that she types for money

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: I could do with much less than that, Mr. Holmes, but you understand that as long as I live at home I don’t wish to be a burden to them, and so they have the use of the money just while I am staying with them. Of course, that is only just for the time. Mr. Windibank draws my interest every quarter and pays it over to mother, and I find that I can do pretty well with what I earn at typewriting. It brings me twopence a sheet, and I can often do from fifteen to twenty sheets in a day.

events.label: Holmes introduces Watson and asks about Hosmer Angel

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: This is my friend, Dr. Watson, before whom you can speak as freely as before myself. Kindly tell us now all about your connection with Mr. Hosmer Angel.

events.label: Mary Sutherland says she met Hosmer Angel at the gasfitters' ball

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: I met him first at the gasfitters’ ball.

events.label: Mary Sutherland explains that Windibank opposed their attendance at outings

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: They used to send father tickets when he was alive, and then afterwards they remembered us, and sent them to mother. Mr. Windibank did not wish us to go. He never did wish us to go anywhere. He would get quite mad if I wanted so much as to join a Sunday-school treat. But this time I was set on going, and I would go; for what right had he to prevent? He said the folk were not fit for us to know, when all father’s friends were to be there. And he said that I had nothing fit to wear, when I had my purple plush that I had never so much as taken out of the drawer.

events.label: Mr. Windibank goes to France on firm business
Miss Mary Sutherland goes to France with her mother and Mr. Hardy
Miss Mary Sutherland meets Mr. Hosmer Angel in France
Mr. Windibank returns from France and is annoyed that Miss Mary Sutherland went to the ball
Mr. Windibank laughs, shrugs, and says there is no use denying anything to a woman

communicates.speaker: mr_windibank
communicates.content: there was no use denying anything to a woman, for she would have her way

events.label: Miss Mary Sutherland meets Mr. Hosmer Angel at the gasfitters' ball
Mr. Hosmer Angel calls next day to ask whether the household got home safe

communicates.speaker: mr_hosmer_angel
communicates.content: if we had got home all safe

events.label: Miss Mary Sutherland and Mr. Hosmer Angel go for two walks
Mr. Windibank returns again from France and Mr. Hosmer Angel can no longer come to the house
Miss Mary Sutherland explains that her father did not like visitors and wanted family circle only

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: father didn't like anything of the sort; he wouldn't have any visitors if he could help it, and he used to say that a woman should be happy in her own family circle

events.label: Miss Mary Sutherland says Mr. Hosmer Angel had made no attempt to see her

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: Mr. Hosmer Angel made no attempt to see you

events.label: Mr. Hosmer Angel writes that it is safer and better not to see each other until Mr. Windibank has gone

communicates.speaker: mr_hosmer_angel
communicates.content: it would be safer and better not to see each other until he had gone

events.label: Miss Mary Sutherland and Mr. Hosmer Angel exchange daily letters
Miss Mary Sutherland and Mr. Hosmer Angel become engaged
Mr. Hosmer Angel is described as a cashier in an office in Leadenhall Street
Mr. Hosmer Angel sleeps on the premises
Miss Mary Sutherland addresses letters to the Leadenhall Street Post Office
Mr. Hosmer Angel refuses typewritten letters and explains why

communicates.speaker: mr_hosmer_angel
communicates.content: if they were sent to the office he would be chaffed by all the other clerks about having letters from a lady, and when I wrote them they seemed to come from me, but when they were typewritten he always felt that the machine had come between us

events.label: Holmes comments that the little things are the most important

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: it has long been an axiom of mine that the little things are infinitely the most important

events.label: Miss Mary Sutherland describes Mr. Hosmer Angel as shy, retiring, gentle, and weak-throated

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: He was a very shy man; he would rather walk with me in the evening than in the daylight; he was very retiring and gentlemanly; his voice was gentle; he had a weak throat from quinsy and swollen glands when young; he was well dressed, neat and plain, and wore tinted glasses against the glare

events.label: Mr. Hosmer Angel returns to the house and proposes marriage before Mr. Windibank comes back
Mr. Hosmer Angel makes Miss Mary Sutherland swear loyalty on the Testament

communicates.speaker: mr_hosmer_angel
communicates.content: whatever happened I would always be true to him

events.label: Miss Mary Sutherland says her mother favored Mr. Hosmer Angel from the first

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: Mother said he was quite right to make me swear, and that it was a sign of his passion; mother was all in his favour from the first and was even fonder of him than I was

events.label: Mary asks about her father before the planned marriage

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: Then, when they talked of marrying within the week, I began to ask about father; but they both said never to mind about father, but just to tell him afterwards, and mother said she would make it all right with him.

events.label: Mary writes to her father at Bordeaux
Mary’s letter to her father arrives back unopened on the wedding morning
Father travels to England before the letter arrives
Mary and Hosmer’s wedding is arranged for Friday at a church
Hosmer arrives with Mary by hansom cab and takes a four-wheeler
Mary and the cabman find Hosmer missing from the four-wheeler
Mary says Hosmer vanished and she has had no news since last Friday

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: That was last Friday, Mr. Holmes, and I have never seen or heard anything since then to throw any light upon what became of him.

events.label: Holmes says Mary has been shamefully treated

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It seems to me that you have been very shamefully treated.

events.label: Hosmer tells Mary to remain true if something unforeseen separates them

communicates.speaker: mr_hosmer_angel
communicates.content: whatever happened, I was to be true; and that even if something quite unforeseen occurred to separate us, I was always to remember that I was pledged to him, and that he would claim his pledge sooner or later.

events.label: Holmes asks whether an unforeseen catastrophe occurred

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Your own opinion is, then, that some unforeseen catastrophe has occurred to him?

events.label: Mary says she has no notion what happened to Hosmer

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: None.

events.label: Holmes asks how Mary’s mother took the matter

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: How did your mother take the matter?

events.label: Mary says her mother was angry and told her not to speak of the matter again

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: She was angry, and said that I was never to speak of the matter again.

events.label: Holmes asks whether Mary told her father

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Did you tell him?

events.label: Mary says she told her father and that he expected to hear of Hosmer again

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: Yes; and he seemed to think, with me, that something had happened, and that I should hear of Hosmer again.

events.label: Mary sobs into a handkerchief
Holmes says he will examine the case

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I shall glance into the case for you, and I have no doubt that we shall reach some definite result. Let the weight of the matter rest upon me now, and do not let your mind dwell upon it further. Above all, try to let Mr. Hosmer Angel vanish from your memory, as he has done from your life.

events.label: Mary Sutherland asks whether she will see Hosmer Angel again

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: Then you don’t think I’ll see him again?

events.label: Mary Sutherland asks what has happened to Hosmer Angel

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: Then what has happened to him?

events.label: Holmes asks for a description and letters

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I should like an accurate description of him and any letters of his which you can spare.

events.label: Mary Sutherland says she advertised for Hosmer Angel and presents the slip and letters

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: I advertised for him in last Saturday’s Chronicle. Here is the slip and here are four letters from him.

events.label: Holmes asks for Mary Sutherland's address and Mr. Angel's address

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: And your address? Mr. Angel’s address you never had, I understand.

events.label: Holmes asks for Mary Sutherland's father's place of business

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Where is your father’s place of business?

events.label: Holmes tells Mary Sutherland to leave the papers and remember his advice

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You have made your statement very clearly. You will leave the papers here, and remember the advice which I have given you. Let the whole incident be a sealed book, and do not allow it to affect your life.

events.label: Mary Sutherland refuses Holmes's advice and declares loyalty to Hosmer Angel

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: You are very kind, Mr. Holmes, but I cannot do that. I shall be true to Hosmer. He shall find me ready when he comes back.

events.label: Mary Sutherland leaves the room after placing the papers on the table
Holmes sits silently, lights his pipe, and rests back in his chair
Holmes remarks on the maiden and her problem

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Quite an interesting study, that maiden. I found her more interesting than her little problem, which is rather a trite one. You will find parallel cases, if you consult my index, in Andover in ’77, and there was something of the sort at The Hague last year. Old as is the idea, however, there were one or two details which were new to me. But the maiden herself was most instructive.

events.label: Watson comments that Holmes read details invisible to him

communicates.speaker: doctor_watson
communicates.content: You appeared to read a good deal upon her which was quite invisible to me.

events.label: Holmes replies that Watson missed what was important and asks for a description

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Not invisible but unnoticed, Watson. You did not know where to look, and so you missed all that was important. I can never bring you to realise the importance of sleeves, the suggestiveness of thumb-nails, or the great issues that may hang from a boot-lace. Now, what did you gather from that woman’s appearance? Describe it.

events.label: Watson describes the woman's appearance

communicates.speaker: doctor_watson
communicates.content: She had a slate-coloured, broad-brimmed straw hat, with a feather of a brickish red. Her jacket was black, with black beads sewn upon it, and a fringe of little black jet ornaments. Her dress was brown, rather darker than coffee colour, with a little purple plush at the neck and sleeves. Her gloves were greyish and were worn through at the right forefinger. Her boots I didn’t observe. She had small round, hanging gold earrings, and a general air of being fairly well-to-do in a vulgar, comfortable, easy-going way.

events.label: Holmes claps and chuckles
Holmes praises Watson's progress in observation and reasoning

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You are coming along wonderfully. You have really done very well indeed. You have missed everything of importance, but you have hit upon the method, and you have a quick eye for colour. Never trust to general impressions, but concentrate yourself upon details. My first glance is always at a woman’s sleeve. In a man it is perhaps better first to take the knee of the trouser.

events.label: Holmes examines the woman's sleeve and sees traces on it
Holmes inspects the woman's face and remarks on her short sight and typewriting

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I ventured a remark upon short sight and typewriting.

events.label: Holmes observes the woman's odd boots and half-buttoned state and infers she came away in a hurry
Watson asks Holmes what else he noticed

communicates.speaker: doctor_watson
communicates.content: And what else?

events.label: Holmes explains that the woman wrote a note before leaving home and had ink-stained glove and finger

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: She had written a note before leaving home but after being fully dressed. Her right glove was torn at the forefinger, and both glove and finger were stained with violet ink. She had written in a hurry and dipped her pen too deep. It must have been this morning.

events.label: Holmes asks Watson to read the advertised description of Mr. Hosmer Angel

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Would you mind reading me the advertised description of Mr. Hosmer Angel?

events.label: Watson reads the printed slip describing Mr. Hosmer Angel

communicates.speaker: doctor_watson
communicates.content: Missing, on the morning of the fourteenth, a gentleman named Hosmer Angel. About five ft. seven in. in height; strongly built, sallow complexion, black hair, a little bald in the centre, bushy, black side-whiskers and moustache; tinted glasses, slight infirmity of speech. Was dressed, when last seen, in black frock-coat faced with silk, black waistcoat, gold Albert chain, and grey Harris tweed trousers, with brown gaiters over elastic-sided boots. Known to have been employed in an office in Leadenhall Street.

events.label: Holmes examines the letters and points out the typewritten signature

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The letters are very commonplace. There is no clue in them to Mr. Angel, save that he quotes Balzac once. They are typewritten. The signature is typewritten. The point about the signature is very suggestive—in fact, we may call it conclusive. I shall write two letters, one to a firm in the City and the other to Mr. Windibank, asking him whether he could meet us here at six o’clock tomorrow evening.

events.label: The speakers agree to wait for the letters' answers

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: we can do nothing until the answers to those letters come, so we may put our little problem upon the shelf for the interim

events.label: Watson reflects on Holmes's reasoning and energy
Watson leaves Holmes and expects Holmes to have clues by the next evening
Watson spends the next day attending a professional case at a sufferer's bedside
Watson travels by hansom cab to Baker Street
Watson finds Holmes alone in an armchair at Baker Street
Watson asks whether Holmes has solved the mystery

communicates.speaker: doctor_watson
communicates.content: Well, have you solved it?

events.label: Holmes answers that he solved the salt question with bisulphate of baryta

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Yes. It was the bisulphate of baryta.

events.label: Watson objects that he meant the mystery

communicates.speaker: doctor_watson
communicates.content: No, no, the mystery!

events.label: Holmes says there was never any mystery and that the scoundrel cannot be reached by law

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I thought of the salt that I have been working upon. There was never any mystery in the matter, though, as I said yesterday, some of the details are of interest. The only drawback is that there is no law, I fear, that can touch the scoundrel.

events.label: Watson asks who the man was and what his object was in deserting Miss Sutherland

communicates.speaker: doctor_watson
communicates.content: Who was he, then, and what was his object in deserting Miss Sutherland?

events.label: A heavy footfall and knock announce Windibank's arrival
Windibank enters the room and sits down
Holmes greets Windibank and asks about the typewritten appointment letter

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Good-evening, Mr. James Windibank. I think that this typewritten letter is from you, in which you made an appointment with me for six o'clock?

events.label: Windibank admits the appointment and explains his lateness and complaints about the matter

communicates.speaker: mr_windibank
communicates.content: Yes, sir. I am afraid that I am a little late, but I am not quite my own master, you know. I am sorry that Miss Sutherland has troubled you about this little matter, for I think it is far better not to wash linen of the sort in public. It was quite against my wishes that she came, but she is a very excitable, impulsive girl, as you may have noticed, and she is not easily controlled when she has made up her mind on a point.

events.label: Holmes discusses typewriter individuality and note characteristics

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It is a curious thing that a typewriter has really quite as much individuality as a man’s handwriting. Unless they are quite new, no two of them write exactly alike. Some letters get more worn than others, and some wear only on one side. Now, you remark in this note of yours, Mr. Windibank, that in every case there is some little slurring over of the ‘e,’ and a slight defect in the tail of the ‘r.’ There are fourteen other characteristics, but those are the more obvious.

events.label: Windibank says the office uses the machine for all correspondence

communicates.speaker: mr_windibank
communicates.content: We do all our correspondence with this machine at the office, and no doubt it is a little worn.

events.label: Holmes describes his study of the typewriter and crime

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I will show you what is really a very interesting study, Mr. Windibank. I think of writing another little monograph some of these days on the typewriter and its relation to crime. It is a subject to which I have devoted some little attention.

events.label: Holmes presents four typewritten letters as coming from the missing man
Windibank rises from his chair and picks up his hat
Windibank says he will not waste time on the talk and asks to be informed if Holmes catches the man

communicates.speaker: mr_windibank
communicates.content: I cannot waste time over this sort of fantastic talk, Mr. Holmes. If you can catch the man, catch him, and let me know when you have done it.

events.label: Holmes turns the key in the door and says he has caught the man

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I let you know, then, that I have caught him!

events.label: Windibank reacts in alarm and demands to know where the man is

communicates.speaker: mr_windibank
communicates.content: What! where?

events.label: Holmes says the situation is too transparent and orders Windibank to sit down

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Oh, it won’t do—really it won’t. There is no possible getting out of it, Mr. Windibank. It is quite too transparent, and it was a very bad compliment when you said that it was impossible for me to solve so simple a question. That’s right! Sit down and let us talk it over.

events.label: Windibank collapses into a chair
Windibank says the matter is not actionable

communicates.speaker: mr_windibank
communicates.content: It’s not actionable.

events.label: Holmes speaks privately about the trick and asks to review the course of events

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I am very much afraid that it is not. But between ourselves, Windibank, it was as cruel and selfish and heartless a trick in a petty way as ever came before me. Now, let me just run over the course of events, and you will contradict me if I go wrong.

events.label: Windibank sits huddled in his chair with his head sunk upon his breast
Holmes begins his account of the events behind the marriage and money

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The man married a woman very much older than himself for her money, and he enjoyed the use of the money of the daughter as long as she lived with them. It was a considerable sum, for people in their position, and the loss of it would have made a serious difference. It was worth an effort to preserve it.

events.label: Mr. Windibank disguises himself as Hosmer Angel to court Miss Sutherland and deter other suitors
Mr. Windibank begins calling on Miss Sutherland as Hosmer Angel
Mr. Windibank and Miss Sutherland meet and become engaged
Mr. Windibank brings Miss Sutherland to the church door and vanishes by the four-wheeler trick
Holmes tells Windibank that he deserves punishment and threatens to use a hunting crop

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The law cannot, as you say, touch you, yet there never was a man who deserved punishment more. If the young lady has a brother or a friend, he ought to lay a whip across your shoulders.

events.label: Mr. Windibank flees down the road
Holmes explains his reasoning about Hosmer Angel and the stepfather

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: There’s a cold-blooded scoundrel. That fellow will rise from crime to crime until he does something very bad, and ends on a gallows. The case has, in some respects, been not entirely devoid of interest. It was obvious from the first that this Mr. Hosmer Angel must have some strong object for his curious conduct, and it was equally clear that the only man who really profited by the incident, as far as we could see, was the stepfather. The two men were never together, but the one always appeared when the other was away. The tinted spectacles, the curious voice, and the bushy whiskers hinted at a disguise. His peculiar action in typewriting his signature inferred that his handwriting was so familiar to her that she would recognise even the smallest sample of it. All these isolated facts, together with many minor ones, all pointed in the same direction.

events.label: Watson asks how Holmes verified the facts

communicates.speaker: doctor_watson
communicates.content: And how did you verify them?

events.label: Holmes explains how he verified the facts

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Having once spotted my man, it was easy to get corroboration. I knew the firm for which this man worked. Having taken the printed description, I eliminated everything from it which could be the result of a disguise—the whiskers, the glasses, the voice—and I sent it to the firm, with a request that they would inform me whether it answered to the description of any of their travellers. I had already noticed the peculiarities of the typewriter, and I wrote to the man himself at his business address asking him if he would come here. As I expected, his reply was typewritten and revealed the same trivial but characteristic defects. The same post brought me a letter from Westhouse & Marbank, of Fenchurch Street, to say that the description tallied in every respect with that of their employee, James Windibank.

events.label: Holmes says he cannot tell Miss Sutherland because she will not believe him

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: If I tell her she will not believe me. You may remember the old Persian saying, “There is danger for him who taketh the tiger cub, and danger also for whoso snatches a delusion from a woman.” There is as much sense in Hafiz as in Horace, and as much knowledge of the world.

clues.significance: Holmes inferred that the newspaper item was not a typical cruelty case because the husband was a teetotaler, there was no other woman, and he threw his false teeth at his wife.
Holmes inferred that the woman's appearance was instructive and that important details could be read from her clothing and accessories.
Holmes inferred short sight and typewriting from the dents made by the pince-nez at either side of the woman's nose.
Holmes inferred that the woman wrote in a hurry and dipped her pen too deep from the violet ink stain on her glove and finger.
Holmes identified the substance that accounted for the chemical result he had been working upon.

Holmes inferred that the same office typewriter produced the letters because the slurring of the ‘e,’ the defect in the tail of the ‘r,’ and the fourteen other characteristics matched across the typewritten letters.
Holmes inferred that the tinted spectacles, curious voice, and bushy whiskers pointed to a disguise.
Holmes inferred that the typewritten signature indicated handwriting familiar to Miss Sutherland.
